title: Air India to Launch India's First UATP Corporate Travel Payment Program
excerpt: The Tata-owned carrier will let companies and travel agencies buy tickets through a single centralized UATP account instead of juggling cards and payment methods for every traveler.
body:
• Air India will become the first airline in India to offer UATP accounts, UATP announced on September 14, letting businesses and travel agencies buy tickets through a single centralized account.
  • The program goes live in the coming months; UATP has established UATP India Private Ltd. in Mumbai and developed a rupee settlement solution to support it.
  • UATP is the airline-owned corporate payments network whose rails handle an estimated 15% of global air-travel payments, per industry reporting by PYMNTS.
  • For Air India, the move advances its Vihaan.AI transformation: cheaper distribution, richer data on corporate spending and deeper ties with travel agencies.

Air India is preparing to become the first airline in India to offer UATP accounts to corporate customers and travel agencies, UATP announced on September 14. The arrangement will let businesses and agencies purchase Air India tickets through a single centralized account rather than juggling cards and payment methods for every traveler.

The shift replaces per-ticket payment chaos with one account: companies get consolidated visibility into travel spend, simpler reconciliation, itemized reporting and tighter payment controls. Air India, in turn, gets cheaper and more direct distribution plus richer data on who is buying and why.

A formal agreement will be announced in the coming months, and the program goes live shortly after, UATP said.

Context & Background: What UATP Is

Most flyers have never heard of UATP. The Universal Air Travel Plan is the oldest payments network in travel — about 83 years old — and it is owned by more than two dozen airlines and operated on their behalf, according to UATP and PYMNTS reporting. Its payment rails handle an estimated 15% of the global air-travel market, with 80% of that business coming from outside the United States.

Here is how it works: airlines issue virtual UATP payment accounts to corporate customers, who receive favorable economics for using those rails. The savings airlines capture — alternative forms of payment run cheaper than traditional credit-card networks — fund tailored corporate offers. The network does not issue cards itself; it manages the messy payment flows that define corporate travel, from last-minute changes and cancellations to add-on fees and currency conversions.

It also sells data tools, DataStream and DataMine, that give issuers and corporate account holders detailed transaction data for travel management — the plumbing that finance teams actually need.

"Through UATP, we are empowering our travel agency partners with a modern payment solution that improves efficiency, visibility, and control across the payment process."

— Nipun Aggarwal, Chief Commercial Officer, Air India

For the India launch, UATP has established UATP India Private Ltd. in Mumbai and developed a settlement solution for the Indian currency — the regulatory and technical groundwork that makes domestic corporate billing practical. "India is a market of significant strategic importance to UATP, and Air India is the ideal partner as the first airline offering UATP in the region," UATP president and CEO Ralph A. Kaiser said in the announcement.

Impact & Analysis

The economics explain why airlines push this. Savings of even 1–2% per transaction are significant for companies spending tens of millions a year on airfare, and for airlines the savings versus credit-card networks are real money. UATP projects India's digital payment transactions will grow from 159 billion in FY2023-24 to 481 billion by FY2028-29, with aviation supporting 7.7 million jobs and 1.5% of GDP — a corporate-travel market too large for Air India to cede to intermediaries.

For corporate travel managers, the practical change is mundane but valuable: one account instead of dozens of cards, standardized reporting, tighter policy enforcement. For Air India, it is distribution leverage — direct corporate relationships reduce dependence on intermediaries — and a differentiator as it courts business traffic against rivals.

The timing fits the carrier's broader overhaul. The Air India Group employs more than 30,000 people, operates over 300 aircraft and has 600 new jets on order. It serves 60 domestic and 51 international destinations across five continents, and the UATP tie-in sits squarely inside its Vihaan.AI transformation, which has already covered fleet renewal, new cabin products and digital systems.

Diaspora Angle

Indian businesses and NRI professionals who fly Air India on US–India and other long-haul routes do much of their booking through corporate travel programs and travel agencies; if their employers enroll, tickets will settle through a single Air India account — less expense-report friction and access to negotiated corporate fares.

What's Next / Looking Ahead

Watch for the formal agreement and the go-live date, the economics Air India offers its first corporate clients, and whether rival Indian carriers follow. If the model works, expect UATP to push beyond tickets — its PAXVIA virtual-card product already covers hotel bookings — and deepen its India footprint.
